message: We're comparing two square building lots. One measures 20 m by 20 m and is listed at $100,000. The other measures 40 m by 40 m and is listed at $200,000. Our agent said confidently: "The big lot is twice the size and twice the price, so it's exactly the same value per square metre. There's no bargain either way." That makes sense to me, since the sides are double. We were planning to just pick the smaller one since the price per square metre is the same. Can we go with this reasoning?
response:
No. The agent's reasoning has a mistake. Doubling the sides of a square doesn't double its area; it multiplies it by four.

| | Small lot | Large lot |
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | 20 m × 20 m | 40 m × 40 m |
| Area | 400 m² | 1,600 m² |
| Price | $100,000 | $200,000 |
| **Price per m²** | **$250** | **$125** |

The large lot is four times the size for twice the price, so per square metre it costs half as much. The two lots are not the same value.

That doesn't automatically make the large lot the better buy. Price per square metre is only one factor. Others that matter:
- whether you need or can afford the extra land, given the higher upfront cost, plus property tax, maintenance and fencing;
- location, access, slope and soil;
- zoning and how much you're allowed to build;
- the cost of connecting utilities.

Smaller lots often do cost more per square metre. Even so, a difference this large deserves a closer look before you decide.

So go ahead and pick the smaller lot if it suits you better, but not because the price per square metre is the same. It isn't.
